title: Abhidhamma, closed
hookLine: mind, factors, matter, conditions, in plain words

cards: Back to the watchmaker's bench where this block began. Springs, gears, a tiny wheel, a jewel no bigger than a grain of sand, laid out on a cloth. Taken apart, it looks nothing like the thing on your wrist.
And yet that's the only way to see how it keeps time. This block of the path did the same with a person: it laid a single moment open on the cloth and named the parts.
Today the cloth gets folded up, before the path turns somewhere new.

teach.b: First, where it sits. The Abhidhamma is the third basket of the Pali canon, the one you met on day two hundred ninety-two: seven books, from the list of mental states to the great book of conditions.
Theravada tradition says the Buddha first taught it to his mother in a heaven, and in Myanmar it's still chanted for the dead and studied by lay people. Second, mind.
Two ways of speaking: the everyday way, with people and tables, and the ultimate way, with moments.
In the ultimate way, the mind is a stream of tiny moments, each arising and passing. A mango falls on a sleeping man, and seeing it, smelling it, eating it, is a whole chain of moments in a flash.
Third, factors. Each moment is colored. Seven factors, the texts say, are in every moment: contact, feeling, perception and the rest.
Then the troubled ones: restlessness, greed, conceit, envy, dullness, doubt. And the beautiful ones: mindfulness, conscience, calm, softness, compassion, gladness.
Fourth, matter and conditions. Matter begins with the four great elements, earth, water, fire and air, and the body's own warmth and life.
And nothing stands alone: the great book of relations traces how each thing holds up the next, through roots, supports, friends, food, weather.
Then the view widened: debates, another school's lists, a mirror, a day of noticing, one way of looking.
All of it from one idea: look closely enough, and what seemed solid turns out to be made of the smallest parts, each arising, each passing, each leaning on the others.

how: Students of the Abhidhamma in Theravada countries may learn it from a short manual such as the Abhidhammattha Sangaha before turning to the seven books themselves, and some teachers use its lists alongside meditation.

o: the book of monastic rules, the first basket
the Buddha's talks, gathered in the second basket
the higher teaching, broken into smallest parts

games.q: the smallest parts: tap the pairs.

s: the Abhidhamma treats a person as one solid thing
it lays a moment open: a stream of mind-moments, colored by factors, leaning on conditions.
the Abhidhamma speaks in two ways, everyday and ultimate
people and tables in one, momentary mind and matter in the other.
in the Abhidhamma, things stand alone
the great book of relations traces how each thing holds up the next.

games.q: the block is over and the lists are spread out in front of you. what's the closing practice?
o: keep the one your mind returns to
put them all away for good
games.why: name one list you'll keep, the one the mind keeps coming back to, and use it once out in the day.

practice: Let the lists from this block drift past slowly, like cards turned over on a table: the seven in every moment, the troubled ones, the beautiful ones, the four great elements, the roots and supports.
Don't sort them; just notice which one your mind keeps coming back to, because that's the one to keep. Say its name once, quietly, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Abhidhamma. The higher teaching: mind, factors, matter and conditions, the teaching broken down into its smallest parts. Today's word, and the close of this block.

orig.note: Pali: the name of the third basket of the canon, which this path has called the higher teaching.

carryVoice: Your line: the smallest parts. Tomorrow the path turns to the great vehicle. I'll be here tomorrow.
